title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Chemical Plants | MPI
description: Mag particle testing for US petrochemical plants: spheres, ammonia and caustic service, nozzles, lifting lugs and pipe racks. Send your list for an MT quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Petrochemical and Chemical Plants in the US
html:
Atlantis NDT travels to US chemical and petrochemical plants to perform magnetic particle inspection on carbon steel and other ferromagnetic equipment: pressure spheres, storage vessels, reactor and column nozzles, process piping welds, pipe rack steel and lifting hardware. We report surface and near-surface cracks to the plant's inspector, who decides on repair. Austenitic stainless, duplex and nickel alloys do not respond to this method and go to penetrant testing. Request an MT inspection quote with your equipment list.

Why chemical plants use MPI

In a chemical complex the carbon steel portion of the asset base is large: LPG and ammonia storage, process vessels, cooling water and utility piping, pipe racks, and the structural steel that carries everything. All of it is welded, much of it sees cyclic loading, and cracks at welds are one of the failure paths that safety programs worry about most. Magnetic particle inspection is the quickest way to check a carbon steel weld for surface-breaking cracks, and it needs less preparation than most methods. The method has a hard limit, though: it works only on ferromagnetic material, so the stainless side of the plant needs liquid penetrant testing for petrochemical plants instead.

Equipment where MT is asked for

  • Pressure spheres and bullets. Welds on LPG, butadiene and similar storage vessels are examined during out-of-service inspections; the internal surface is often examined with wet fluorescent particles for sensitivity.
  • Ammonia storage and refrigerated tanks. Carbon steel in anhydrous ammonia service is susceptible to stress corrosion cracking at welds when oxygen or contamination is present. Wet fluorescent magnetic particle examination of welds is a recognized way to look for it.
  • Caustic and amine systems. Carbon steel piping and vessels in caustic service can crack near welds that were never stress relieved; MT is the standard check after heat tracing or temperature excursions.
  • Column and reactor nozzles. Nozzle-to-shell welds and reinforcement pad welds, particularly after repairs.
  • Heavy lifting hardware. Lugs, trunnions and pad eyes on vessels and modules are examined before lifts during maintenance campaigns. The owner's lifting specification, which may reference ASME BTH-1 for below-the-hook devices, sets the criteria.
  • Pipe racks and supports. Weld cracking at support attachments, shoe welds and guides, often triggered by vibration or thermal cycling.

The plant's inspector or engineer picks the scope based on the damage mechanism and the code. The relevant plant-level drivers are OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 mechanical integrity requirements and the equivalent obligations of the EPA Risk Management Program under 40 CFR Part 68, with ASME Section VIII, B31.3 and, where the owner has adopted them, API 510 and API 570 shaping what gets examined and when.

Technique details that matter in chemical service

  • Method set-up. AC yoke work follows ASME Section V Article 7 and ASTM E709. The yoke's lifting power is checked before use, with the results recorded on the report.
  • Field direction. Each weld is examined with the field in two roughly perpendicular directions so cracks of any orientation are seen.
  • Particles. We use dry powder on rough, warm welds and wet suspension, visible or fluorescent, for fine cracking or for critical service such as ammonia. Contrast paint may be applied lightly to improve visibility of visible-color particles on dark metal.
  • Surface and coatings. Welds have to be accessible and reasonably clean. Heavy scale, spatter and thick paint reduce sensitivity, and the procedure sets how much coating is acceptable.
  • Product protection. In polymer and specialty chemical sites, particle residue is wiped off completely so nothing reaches the process, and oil-based carriers are kept away from open product contact surfaces. Tell us what the equipment is used for and we will pick a carrier that suits.
  • Temperature. Wet suspensions have temperature limits; hot surfaces may need dry powder or a procedure demonstrated for that temperature.
  • Ignition control. Yokes avoid the open arcing that prods produce, which matters in classified areas. Where a permit allows prods, it is stated on the report.

Material check before we start

Chemical plants mix metals, and a pipe that looks like carbon steel may be an alloy. A quick magnet test tells us whether a part will respond, but it is not a material identification. If the plant needs alloy verification, positive material identification is a separate scope that we do not provide here. We rely on the plant's drawings and specifications, and flag it if a part fails to hold the yoke as expected, so the right method can be swapped in before we write a clean report on a part that was never examinable.

Shutdown sequencing for sphere and tank work

Out-of-service inspection of a large storage vessel is a chain of dependent jobs: emptying, cleaning, gas-freeing, scaffolding, blasting or grinding, examination, repair, re-examination and closing up. MT sits in the middle, and the quality of everything before it decides how much we can see. A weld that was only wire-brushed hides cracks that a light blast would reveal. We ask for a short pre-job walk with your inspector to look at a sample weld, agree on the surface standard and confirm lighting, so the crew does not arrive to find surfaces that cannot be examined.

Corroded process pipingNoNoFirst choice

For thickness work see ultrasonic testing for petrochemical plants. Our MT versus PT guide and complete MT guide give the reasoning in more detail, and the weld inspection page shows where surface methods fit alongside others.

Cracking mechanisms behind the requests

API 571 is the usual reference for what damages equipment in these plants, and a few mechanisms explain most MT requests. Stress corrosion cracking needs three things together: a susceptible material, a corrosive environment and tensile stress, and welds supply the stress. Fatigue cracking starts where a vibrating or cycling part meets a stress concentration, often a weld toe on a support or branch. Brittle fracture is a concern for carbon steel in cold service, such as parts of ethylene and refrigerated storage systems, where a surface crack can grow quickly if the metal is below its transition temperature. In each case, MT is not the root-cause tool; it is how the owner finds out whether a crack is present, how long, and where, so the engineer can choose what to do.

The owner's engineering group decides whether a crack-like indication can be ground out, repaired, monitored or means the vessel needs replacement. If grinding removes a defect, a follow-up MT confirms it is gone and the remaining thickness is checked by UT, so the weld is not left thinner than the code allows.

Who accepts the result

Acceptance is set by the code or specification the plant names: ASME B31.3 for piping, Section VIII for vessels, API 510 or API 570 for in-service repairs the plant has adopted. The Level II technician reports every indication with its position and size and records the criteria cited. The plant's inspector or engineer accepts, rejects or orders repair. Where a crack is found, the report shows its location on a sketch so the repair crew can find it again, and we re-examine after repair if the scope includes it. Under SNT-TC-1A an ASNT Level III approves the technique and reviews the report before it is issued.

Planning inside an operating complex

Many plants are continuous processes with infrequent outages, and the chemical sites near the Gulf, the Ohio River and the Great Lakes schedule major work in tight windows. We mobilize for the agreed scope, and the site's permit system covers hot work, confined-space entry and gas testing. Spheres and large tanks mean confined-space entry and often scaffolding, set up by the owner's contractors. Fluorescent MT needs a darkened area, which can be created with a tent or shade inside a vessel or blocked off at ground level. Credentials such as TWIC are needed at port-adjacent sites. Because chemicals may be toxic, expect added restrictions on personal protective equipment and on how long a technician can work in one area. See the pressure vessel inspection page and tank inspection page for how these scopes are usually organized.

What the report contains

  • Equipment tag, weld number and location, tied to the owner's drawing.
  • Procedure and revision, code section and acceptance criteria cited.
  • Yoke ID and lift verification, particle type, brand and lot, and whether fluorescent.
  • Measured visible-light or ultraviolet intensity at the examined area.
  • Technician name and level, with the ASNT Level III reviewer's name.
  • Indications with type, position, size and a sketch, and accept or reject.
  • Areas not examined, with the reason, and any need for a different method.

What to send us for a quote

  • Equipment list with tags and drawings, or a weld map.
  • Base metal, thickness and service, including ammonia, caustic or amine.
  • Welds or linear feet to examine, and the governing code or specification.
  • Surface condition, coating and insulation status, temperature.
  • Whether internal access is needed and what confined-space rules apply.
  • Site address, credentials, orientation, and your work window.

Where we work in the US for chemical plants

  • Houston: chemical and polymer plants along the Ship Channel.
  • Beaumont: Southeast Texas plants with large sphere and tank farms.
  • Baton Rouge: river corridor chemicals and fertilizer plants.
  • Lake Charles: olefins and chemical complexes in southwest Louisiana.
  • Corpus Christi: coastal chemical and energy sites.
  • New Orleans: river chemical plants and terminals.
  • Louisville: the Ohio River chemical district.
  • Chicago: chemical and polymer plants of the Great Lakes region.

Training your own technicians

Plants that want in-house capability can start with MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 theory, plus the magnetic particle simulator for practice. Your company certifies its own people under SNT-TC-1A from a written practice; our technical procedure development and written practice development services support that. See the manufacturing NDT training page for sector programs, or the national magnetic particle testing page.

What we do not do

Radiography is outside our scope in the United States, as are specialist techniques beyond this page, alloy identification and the authorized inspector's role of record. Remaining-life decisions stay with your engineer. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

faq.q: Can MT be used on stainless steel piping in a chemical plant?
faq.a: Not on austenitic stainless or most duplex grades, because they do not carry a magnetic field. Those welds go to liquid penetrant. MT covers the carbon steel and ferritic parts of the same plant.

faq.q: Can you inspect ammonia or LPG spheres?
faq.a: Yes, as part of an out-of-service inspection scope, with the site's confined-space and gas-free permits in place. Welds are examined with wet fluorescent or visible particles as the procedure specifies, and the owner's inspector reviews the results.

faq.q: What do you need to quote MT in a chemical plant?
faq.a: An equipment list or weld map, base metal, service, quantity, the governing code, surface and coating condition, temperature, access and your outage dates. Special concerns about product contamination help us choose the carrier.
The plant's inspector or engineer does, against the code in the procedure. Our Level II technician reports each indication, and an ASNT Level III reviews the report before it is issued.

faq.q: Does MT damage or contaminate process equipment?
faq.a: Not when done properly. We remove particles and suspension afterward, choose carriers suited to the equipment, and avoid leaving anything on surfaces that contact the product. Tell us if the equipment is used for high-purity service.

faq.q: Is magnetic particle inspection safe in a classified area?
faq.a: A yoke avoids the arcing that prods can create, which suits classified areas. The site's hot work and permit rules still apply, and the permit type is recorded on the report.

No. It finds cracks and certain other surface and near-surface discontinuities. For wall loss, we use ultrasonic thickness testing, often in the same visit as the weld examination, under a separate procedure.

faq.q: Will you examine lifting lugs before a heavy lift?
faq.a: Yes. Lug and trunnion welds are common MT targets, and the owner's lifting specification sets criteria. We report cracks and non-relevant indications, but the lift plan stays with your engineer.

faq.q: Do you cover plants outside the Gulf Coast?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your site anywhere in the United States, and the crew can be assembled for Ohio River, Great Lakes and East Coast plants as well.
